ABSTRACT
Privacy-preserving medical inference must balance data locality, diagnostic reliability, and deployment
efficiency. This paper presents EcoFair, a simulated vertically partitioned inference framework for
dermatological diagnosis in which raw image and tabular data remain local and only modality-specific
embeddings are transmitted for server-side multimodal fusion. EcoFair introduces a lightweight-
first routing mechanism that selectively activates a heavier image encoder when local uncertainty or
metadata-derived clinical risk indicates that additional computation is warranted. The routing decision
combines predictive uncertainty, a safe–danger probability gap, and a tabular neurosymbolic risk score
derived from patient age and lesion localisation. Experiments on three dermatology benchmarks show
that EcoFair can substantially reduce edge-side inference energy in representative model pairings
while remaining competitive in classification performance. The results further indicate that selective
routing can improve subgroup-sensitive malignant-case behaviour in representative settings without
modifying the global training objective. These findings position EcoFair as a practical framework for
privacy-preserving and energy-aware medical inference under edge deployment constraints.
KeywordsPrivacy-preserving medical AI ·vertically partitioned inference ·edge–cloud computing ·dynamic routing ·
trustworthy AI·algorithmic fairness·neurosymbolic risk modelling
1 Introduction
The transition towards decentralised digital infrastructures has reshaped how sensitive information is processed, shared,
and utilised across institutional and geographic boundaries. In highly regulated sectors such as healthcare, governed
by frameworks including HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) and GDPR (General Data
Protection Regulation), data can no longer be indiscriminately aggregated into centralised repositories [ 1]. In addition,
the risks associated with single-point-of-failure breaches, unauthorised access, and loss of data sovereignty have
heightened the importance of privacy-preserving decentralised computation. In this setting, predictive value must be
extracted and exchanged without exposing raw digital assets to external parties. This requirement is especially important
in image-based medical applications, where high-resolution images may contain identifiable biometric information
while remaining essential for accurate diagnosis. In the clinical setting considered in this study, a dermatological client
processes skin lesion images, a tabular details stores demographic metadata, and a central server performs multimodal
fusion on intermediate representations. By constraining communication to learned embeddings rather than raw pixels or

It is also observed that vertically partitioned learning architectures have emerged as a practical approach for privacy-
preserving collaborative inference across data silos that hold complementary information about the same patient
population, particularly in healthcare settings where images, metadata, and clinical records may be distributed across
different parties [ 2]. In such settings, vertically partitioned learning offers a natural way to balance predictive utility with
data locality by allowing each party to retain raw inputs while contributing intermediate representations for downstream
inference [ 3,4]. Despite these privacy benefits, real-world deployment introduces additional system-level constraints
where the repeated exchange and processing of representations between edge devices and cloud servers can impose
substantial energy cost, which is problematic for mobile dermatoscopes and resource-constrained clinical settings [ 5].
Existing responses, including quantisation, pruning, and knowledge distillation, can reduce computational burden but
may also weaken representational quality and downstream reliability [ 6]. Besides, in safety-critical medical applications,
energy efficiency cannot be pursued in isolation if it disproportionately degrades performance on clinically important or
demographically vulnerable cases.
EcoFair is designed to address these challenges in a unified post-deployment setting. Rather than presenting an end-to-
end vertically partitioned training pipeline, this work studies a simulated vertically partitioned inference architecture
in which raw image and tabular data remain local, only modality-specific embeddings are transmitted to the server,
and a routing mechanism determines whether inference can be completed using the lightweight image encoder alone
or whether the heavier image encoder must also be activated before multimodal fusion. To examine this deployment
behaviour beyond a single fixed backbone choice, EcoFair is evaluated using multiple pretrained lightweight and
heavyweight image encoders spanning moderate, strong, and extreme compute disparities, including MobileNetV2,
MobileNetV3Small, ResNet50, DenseNet201, and EfficientNetB6. The aim is to improve deployment efficiency while
preserving clinical utility and subgroup-aware safety. Accordingly, this study is guided by the following research
questions:
1.RQ1:How can decentralised medical inference reduce edge-side energy consumption without transmitting
raw biometric data to a central server?
2.RQ2:How can dynamic routing incorporate explicit clinical risk to improve safety when local model
confidence is unreliable?
3.RQ3:To what extent can post-hoc routing improve subgroup-sensitive diagnostic performance without
modifying the global training objective?
In response to these questions, this paper makes the following contributions:
•To address RQ1, we propose a privacy-preserving vertically partitioned inference framework in which raw
image and tabular data remain local and only modality-specific embeddings are exchanged. Within this setting,
EcoFair introduces an energy-aware routing strategy for reducing unnecessary use of the heavier cloud-assisted
image pathway.
•To address RQ2, we combine predictive uncertainty with a tabular neurosymbolic risk score based on patient
age and lesion localisation, providing an interpretable routing signal for clinically higher-risk cases.
• To address RQ3, we investigate whether routing-based escalation can improve subgroup-sensitive diagnostic
behaviour post hoc, particularly for clinically important malignant cases, without altering the global loss
formulation.
The rest of this paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 presents the EcoFair
methodology, including the vertically partitioned inference setting, routing mechanism, and tabular neurosymbolic risk
design. Section 4 reports the experimental evaluation across energy, classification, and fairness perspectives. Section 5
discusses the main findings of this work. Section 6 outlines limitations of the current study and directions for future
research, and Section 7 concludes the paper.
2 Related Work
The development of secure, efficient, and fair decentralised artificial intelligence (AI) has motivated substantial research
across several intersecting areas of computer science. To position EcoFair within this landscape, this section reviews
relevant work on privacy-preserving data exchange, decentralised system optimisation, and fairness-aware medical AI.
A central requirement in cross-institutional collaborative computing is the preservation of data sovereignty and privacy
during information exchange. Recent works have examined secure and auditable infrastructures for controlled cross-

domain data sharing. For example, Zhanget al.[ 7] introduced the Secure Auditable Sharing Protocol together with
a Reputation-driven Proactive Sharing Mechanism to support trustworthy cohort-data exchange across isolated data
centres. Related discussions in Web 3.0 literature have likewise emphasised the importance of moving towards read–
write–own paradigms for user-controlled data management [ 8]. Within machine learning, vertically partitioned federated
settings provide a natural mechanism for privacy-preserving collaboration when different parties hold complementary
attributes of the same individuals, enabling joint predictive modelling without direct raw-data disclosure [ 2,4,3]. In
this context, EcoFair is aligned with privacy-preserving vertically partitioned inference frameworks that are increasingly
advocated for clinical use [ 9], while focusing specifically on post-deployment optimisation rather than end-to-end
federated training.
The deployment of deep models in decentralised and edge environments introduces additional constraints related
to energy, latency, and computational capacity [ 10]. A recent work has sought to mitigate these bottlenecks in
Split Learning architectures by dynamically regulating local computation to handle resource heterogeneity [ 11].
EcoFair complements this system-level focus by addressing post-deployment energy efficiency alongside demographic
fairness. Persistent reliance on remote processing can be prohibitive for battery-constrained clinical devices and
resource-limited healthcare settings. To address this, prior works have explored model compression, lightweight
architectures, and adaptive computation strategies to make dermatological classification viable on resource-constrained
edge devices [ 12,13,14]. Likewise, dynamic routing has emerged as a useful mechanism for selectively allocating
computational effort based on input difficulty or model confidence, thereby mitigating the computational waste of
network "overthinking" on simpler samples [ 15]. In a related direction, Qasimet al.[ 16] examined the sustainability of
federated networks and highlighted the trade-off between model complexity and energy cost. However, many routing
strategies rely primarily on confidence thresholds that may be poorly calibrated in deep neural networks [ 17]. EcoFair
builds on this line of work by combining uncertainty-based routing with an explicit metadata-driven clinical risk signal,
thereby linking deployment efficiency to clinically meaningful decision support.
In medical AI, trustworthiness requires more than average predictive performance. Deployed systems must remain
clinically reliable across demographic groups, avoid amplifying historical biases, and provide reasoning signals that
can support scrutiny in safety-critical settings [ 18,19,20]. In dermatology, one of the fields within the medical
system, unfair behaviour may appear as reduced malignant-case sensitivity for minority subgroups or atypical lesion
presentations, highlighting the need to evaluate fairness robustly across diverse skin tones [ 21,22,23]. At the same
time, neurosymbolic methods have gained attention as a way to incorporate structured domain knowledge into learning
systems and improve interpretability [ 24]. For example, the ZTID-IoV framework applied neurosymbolic design
principles to interpretable zero-trust intrusion detection in decentralised vehicular networks [ 25]. EcoFair adopts a
related principle in the medical setting by integrating neural image-based prediction with a symbolic risk score derived
from explicit patient metadata, and by using this signal to guide post-deployment routing decisions under privacy and
energy constraints.
Taken together, these limitations define the problem addressed in this paper: how to support privacy-preserving medical
inference under edge deployment constraints while avoiding disproportionate degradation on clinically important
and demographically vulnerable cases. In EcoFair, fairness is viewed through the malignant-case Equal Opportunity
perspective, with particular emphasis on improving the worst-group True Positive Rate (WG-TPR) and reducing the
subgroup TPR gap. Existing efficiency-oriented approaches in decentralised and edge AI largely prioritise energy
reduction, compression, or routing economy, but they typically provide limited analysis of whether these savings
are achieved at the expense of subgroup-sensitive diagnostic reliability [ 26]. EcoFair is motivated by this gap and
studies whether routing can jointly improve deployment efficiency and subgroup-aware safety in a vertically partitioned
inference setting.
3 Methodology
EcoFair operationalises the central premise of this study: privacy-preserving medical inference should not be treated
solely as a communication problem, but as a joint systems problem involving representation exchange, adaptive
computation, clinically informed decision support, and subgroup-aware evaluation under edge deployment constraints.
3.1 Formulation of the VFL Environment
EcoFair is formulated as a simulated vertically partitioned medical inference architecture designed to preserve data
locality while enabling multimodal diagnosis. The system follows an Edge-to-Edge-to-Cloud topology with two local
clients and one central server. Party A1 acts as the image client and processes raw dermatological images captured at
the edge. Party A2 acts as the tabular client and processes patient metadata available locally, such as age and lesion
localisation. Party B denotes the central server, which receives modality-specific embeddings and performs multimodal

raw image pixels or raw tabular attributes beyond their originating clients. Fig. 1 illustrates the full EcoFair workflow.
For empirical evaluation, EcoFair is studied in a simulated deployment setting using a centralised 5-fold cross-validation
pipeline. This setup is intended to model routing behaviour, privacy-preserving representation exchange, and edge-side
energy consumption, rather than to implement end-to-end federated training or measure real network latency. On the
image side, Party A1 first computes a lightweight image embedding and the associated routing signals derived from the
local predictive distribution. Based on these signals, the heavier image encoder is either kept inactive or additionally
activated on the same client. On the tabular side, Party A2 independently computes a tabular embedding together
with a metadata-driven risk score. The server then receives the resulting modality-specific embeddings and performs
multimodal fusion for the final prediction.
Privacy preservation in EcoFair follows directly from this architectural constraint. Raw image and tabular inputs remain
local to their respective clients, while only learned intermediate representations are transmitted for downstream fusion.
This design reduces direct exposure of sensitive biometric and demographic information without relying on explicit
cryptographic protocols or injected differential noise at inference time [27].

3.3 Tabular Neurosymbolic Risk Score
Predictive uncertainty alone is not always sufficient for safe routing in clinical settings, since neural models may still
produce confident but incorrect predictions. To reduce this risk, EcoFair augments the routing mechanism with a
tabular neurosymbolic risk score derived from explicit patient metadata [ 31,20]. This component provides a simple and
auditable symbolic signal that operates alongside the image-based uncertainty measures.
The tabular client, Party A2, processes metadata variables that are clinically associated with malignancy risk, specifically
patient age and anatomical site. Lesion localisation is included not only as an anatomical descriptor, but also because
body-site risk patterns in cutaneous melanoma are known to vary with differential ultraviolet exposure and related
epidemiological factors, although this relationship is not uniform across all melanoma subtypes [ 32,33]. Rather

3.4 Fairness-Aware Routing Mechanism
The final methodological component of EcoFair addresses subgroup-sensitive reliability in deployment. In standard
training settings, optimisation is typically driven by aggregate objective functions, which can mask systematic disparities
across demographic groups and clinically atypical cases [ 35]. In medical diagnosis, this may appear as reduced
sensitivity for underrepresented cohorts even when overall performance remains acceptable. However, EcoFair departs
from conventional fairness -inducing approaches as it does not impose fairness through an additional loss term or
constrained optimisation objective during training. Instead, it examines whether fairness can be improved post hoc
through routing behaviour at inference time. The central idea is that samples associated with higher uncertainty,
narrower safe–danger separation, or elevated metadata-derived risk are more likely to correspond to cases for which
lightweight-only inference is less reliable. By selectively activating the heavier image pathway for such cases, EcoFair
provides an operational mechanism for reducing failure on clinically important and subgroup-sensitive samples.

4.1 Evaluation Setup and Protocol
The evaluation uses three publicly available dermatology benchmarks: HAM10000 [ 37], PAD-UFES-20 [ 38], and
BCN20000 [ 39]. These datasets were selected because they collectively capture clinically relevant heterogeneity
in image acquisition conditions, demographic composition, and label imbalance. In particular, PAD-UFES-20 and
BCN20000 introduce stronger out-of-distribution variation than HAM10000, while all three datasets reflect the
imbalance patterns commonly observed in real-world dermatological classification tasks [ 40]. This makes them suitable
for evaluating not only predictive performance, but also the deployment behaviour of routing-based systems under
varying difficulty and subgroup composition.
To support a principled analysis of deployment trade-offs, EcoFair does not rely on a single fixed image backbone.
Instead, a broader screening stage is first used to profile multiple candidate encoders, after which three representative
lite-heavy model pairs are selected for detailed framework-level evaluation. This design allows the experiments to
examine EcoFair under moderate, strong, and extreme compute disparities between lightweight and heavyweight image
pathways. The tabular neurosymbolic risk score is calibrated from the training-fold metadata. Fig. 2 provides the
empirical motivation for this symbolic prior by showing that malignancy prevalence is not uniform across age brackets
or anatomical sites within HAM10000, thereby supporting the use of age and lesion localisation as metadata-driven
routing signals.

4.2 Backbone Screening for Edge–Cloud Deployment
To ensure that the architectural choices used in the EcoFair routing framework are principled rather than ad hoc,
a comprehensive screening of ten widely used convolutional backbones was first conducted. For each architecture,
deployment-oriented characteristics including parameter count, model size, embedding dimensionality, inference latency,
GPU memory footprint, and energy consumption per sample were empirically measured during feature extraction.
These measurements characterise the computational behaviour of each encoder independently of the routing mechanism
and provide an objective basis for selecting representative model combinations for subsequent framework evaluation.
To accurately quantify the computational cost of the feature extraction and inference phases, GPU energy consumption
was dynamically tracked using pynvml, the official Python interface for the NVIDIA Management Library (NVML)
[41]. This approach directly polls hardware-level power sensors, providing a highly accurate and widely validated
standard for energy measurement in deep learning pipelines [42].

4.3 Optimisation of Decentralised Energy Consumption
A primary deployment constraint in edge-based medical inference is the energy cost associated with image processing
under limited on-device resources. In EcoFair, this cost is determined by whether inference proceeds with the lightweight
image encoder alone or whether the heavier image encoder is additionally activated for the same sample before
multimodal fusion. The routing mechanism, therefore, acts directly on the dominant source of variable computation in
the image client and provides a controllable trade-off between efficiency and diagnostic safety.
Table 2 summarises the empirical per-sample energy consumption and routing statistics for the three selected model
pairs across the evaluated datasets. The results show that the energy behaviour of EcoFair is strongly pair-dependent. On
HAM10000, all three pairs achieve a reduction in energy consumption relative to their corresponding heavy baselines,
with savings ranging from 28.09% for MobileNetV2–ResNet50 to 68.09% for MobileNetV3Small–EfficientNetB6. This
confirms that selective heavy-model activation can substantially reduce inference cost when a meaningful computational
gap exists between the lightweight and heavyweight pathways.

4.5 Subgroup-Sensitive Fairness
Subgroup-sensitive fairness is a central requirement in medical deployment because acceptable average performance
can still conceal systematic failure on vulnerable cohorts. In this study, fairness is evaluated primarily through the
Equal Opportunity perspective, which examines parity in True Positive Rate (TPR) across demographic subgroups for
clinically important malignant cases [ 43]. Under this criterion, a system is considered more equitable when it improves
worst-group sensitivity and reduces disparity across subgroups, rather than merely increasing average performance on
the dominant population.
EcoFair does not enforce fairness through a modified training objective or an explicit fairness penalty. Instead, it
investigates whether fairness can be improved post hoc through routing behaviour at inference time. Samples associated
with higher uncertainty, narrower safe–danger separation, or elevated metadata-derived risk are more likely to be difficult
for lightweight-only inference and are therefore more likely to trigger selective heavy-model activation. As shown in
Fig. 4 and summarised in Table 4, the fairness benefit of EcoFair should therefore be interpreted as a deployment-time

5 Discussion
The empirical results position EcoFair as a deployment-oriented framework rather than a universally dominant classifier.
Across the evaluated datasets, its benefit depends on the interaction between routing policy, dataset difficulty, and the
computational disparity between lightweight and heavyweight image pathways. The strongest results are observed when
routing operates over a sufficiently meaningful compute gap, allowing selective heavy-model activation to improve
classification balance and subgroup-sensitive behaviour while still reducing inference cost in representative settings.
A second important finding is that fairness improvement should be interpreted as a deployment-time property of the rout-
ing policy rather than as a guarantee induced by training. EcoFair does not enforce subgroup parity through constrained
optimisation or loss modification. Instead, it improves worst-group malignant-case behaviour in representative settings
by identifying uncertain or clinically higher-risk cases and escalating them selectively. This makes the framework
particularly relevant for practical medical AI deployment, where average predictive performance alone is not sufficient.
At the same time, the results show that the framework is not uniformly optimal across all model pairings and datasets.
More challenging data distributions increase routing frequency, which can reduce the net efficiency advantage for some
backbone combinations. This is an important outcome in itself, because it shows that backbone disparity and routing
design must be considered jointly when assessing the usefulness of selective inference in privacy-preserving medical
systems.
6 Future Work
Several directions remain for future investigation. First, the current evaluation is conducted in a simulated vertically
partitioned inference setting rather than on a physical distributed deployment. A natural next step is to implement
EcoFair on real edge hardware and embedded platforms in order to measure end-to-end latency, communication
overhead, and energy usage under practical operating conditions.
Second, the current framework relies on the availability and quality of local tabular metadata. Future work should
therefore examine the robustness of the neurosymbolic risk component under missing, corrupted, or biased metadata
and investigate more reliable strategies for metadata validation and uncertainty-aware tabular reasoning.
Finally, the present results show that the effectiveness of EcoFair is pair-dependent. Future work should extend the
framework to broader backbone families, stronger calibration strategies, and adaptive routing policies that are more
explicitly optimised for joint energy, performance, and subgroup-sensitive fairness across heterogeneous deployment
environments.
7 Conclusion
The development of practical digital healthcare infrastructures depends on balancing privacy preservation, diagnostic
reliability, and deployment efficiency. In this work, EcoFair has been studied as a simulated vertically partitioned
inference framework designed to address these objectives jointly. The results show that privacy-preserving multimodal
inference can be combined with selective heavy-model activation to support clinically meaningful deployment trade-offs
without transmitting raw image or tabular data beyond their originating clients.
With respect to RQ1 and RQ2, EcoFair demonstrates that lightweight-first inference, uncertainty-aware routing,
and metadata-driven neurosymbolic risk scoring can reduce unnecessary heavy-model activation while preserving a
mechanism for clinically informed escalation. The empirical results further show that the efficiency benefit of this design
is pair-dependent: meaningful energy savings are achieved when the computational disparity between lightweight and
heavyweight pathways is sufficiently large, while more modest pairings offer weaker efficiency gains.
With respect to RQ3, the results indicate that routing can also improve subgroup-sensitive behaviour at deployment time
without modifying the global training objective. Although this fairness benefit is not uniform across all model pairs and

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
This partial document introduces "EcoFair," a framework for privacy-preserving and energy-aware medical inference in a vertically partitioned setting, specifically for dermatological diagnosis. The main points covered are:

*   **Privacy Preservation:** Raw medical data (images and tabular metadata) remains local to the client, with only modality-specific embeddings transmitted for server-side processing. This addresses concerns related to HIPAA and GDPR, and the risks of centralized data aggregation.
*   **Energy Efficiency:** EcoFair aims to reduce energy consumption on edge devices by introducing a "lightweight-first" routing mechanism. This mechanism selectively activates a more computationally intensive image encoder only when local uncertainty or clinical risk indicates it's necessary.
*   **Trustworthiness and Reliability:** The framework balances privacy and energy efficiency with diagnostic reliability. It incorporates predictive uncertainty and a neurosymbolic risk score (derived from patient age and lesion location) to guide the routing decision, ensuring that higher-risk cases receive more thorough analysis.
*   **Vertically Partitioned Inference:** The system operates in a vertically partitioned manner, where different data modalities (image and tabular) are processed locally before intermediate representations are fused on a central server.
*   **Algorithmic Fairness:** The research investigates whether selective routing can improve subgroup-sensitive diagnostic performance, particularly for clinically important malignant cases, without altering the global training objective.
*   **Research Questions:** The paper addresses three key research questions regarding energy reduction in decentralized inference, incorporating clinical risk for safety, and improving subgroup-sensitive performance through post-hoc routing.
*   **Contributions:** The document outlines its contributions in proposing the privacy-preserving framework, the energy-aware routing strategy, the combination of uncertainty and risk for routing, and the investigation of post-hoc routing for fairness.

structure.title: RQ1:How can decentralised medical inference reduce edge-side energy consumption without transmitting raw biometric data to a central server?
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses privacy-preserving, vertically partitioned learning architectures, particularly for healthcare settings.
